items.title: We Found The Oldest Pub In London
items.description:

Learn about the history of pubs in London and join historian Matt Lewis and drinking buddy Kyle Cairns on a historical pub crawl.

15:21 The City of York

items.why_watch: Historian Matt Lewis physically walks through four of London's most historically layered pubs — including Ye Olde Mitre, tucked in a Holborn alleyway and dating to 1546 — explaining what each building reveals about the city's social and political past. It's a pub crawl with genuine historical commentary rather than just atmosphere. A Google Maps list is included if you want to replicate the route yourself.

items.title: Reckless Ben Answers The Web's Most Searched Questions
items.description:
Reckless Ben visits WIRED to answer his most searched questions on Google. What is the Reckless Ben Lego scandal? Does Reckless Ben have a law degree? Why did Reckless Ben start YouTube? Answers to these questions and many more await on Reckless Ben’s WIRED Autocomplete Interview.

Watch more from WIRED | Autocomplete Interview: https://www.youtube.com/show/VLPLibNZv5Zd0dwjZFCTVZ8QdKq194CkwXjo?sbp=QAE%3D 

#RecklessBen #Autocomplete #WIRED

Still haven’t subscribed to WIRED on YouTube? ►► http:/
items.why_watch: WIRED's Autocomplete Interview format works best when the subject is genuinely obscure enough that the questions feel surprising, and Reckless Ben — a YouTuber apparently entangled in a Lego scandal and possibly holding a law degree — fits that bill. It's a quick, low-stakes way to get up to speed on a creator you may have been vaguely aware of. The format keeps things moving, so there's no real filler.

items.title: Who ACTUALLY Makes The Best Philly Cheesesteak?
items.description:
According to those in the know, the best cheesesteak in the world is the one you get at Pat's King of Steaks in Philadelphia... or possibly Geno's Steaks, also in Philadelphia and not coincidentally located just steps away from Pat's. Yes, for decades, Pat’s and Geno’s have stood across the street from each other, turning a simple sandwich into a Philly institution. But how did this legendary cheesesteak rivalry begin? And why does choosing the “right” side still matter so much?

In this episode
items.why_watch: Weird History Food digs into the actual origin story behind the Pat's vs. Geno's rivalry, which turns out to be less about the sandwiches and more about Philadelphia identity, family feuds, and the way a city decides what counts as authentic. If you've ever been handed strong opinions about cheesesteak without much context, this is where the context lives. It covers the history without losing sight of the food.

themes.name: Actually, You've Got It Wrong
themes.tagline: The physics of force, the logic of circuits — turns out the obvious explanation was never quite right.

items.title: Binary Adder - Carry Skip Adder (Carry bypass adder)
items.description:
This video is about the Carry Skip adder which is an adder faster than the conventional ripple carry adder.

Playlist about binary operation: adders, subtractors, division, multiplier
https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLnAxReCloSeTrpY-9q7ECY8ju8Fpi1mzP&si=FhB614G46tgH1niV
items.why_watch: This short video explains the Carry Skip Adder — a specific hardware optimization that speeds up binary addition by bypassing carry propagation under certain conditions — with clear diagrams and minimal fluff. If you're working through digital logic or computer architecture and found ripple carry adders slow to click conceptually, this fills the gap efficiently. At under eight minutes, it respects the fact that this is a narrow topic with a narrow audience.

items.title: Can You Feel Force?
items.description: It's often taught to us in physics that you can "feel a force". But what do statements about feeling force even mean, and are they accurate? The answer will surprise you. A follow-up video to "Why Solutions to the Twin Paradox are Wrong."
items.why_watch: The video challenges the common physics-class claim that you "feel a force," arguing that what you actually perceive is something more specific — and that getting this wrong leads to real conceptual muddles in understanding mechanics. It's a follow-up to a video on the Twin Paradox, so the channel is clearly interested in where physics intuition quietly breaks down. The question sounds trivial until you realize the answer requires rethinking what sensation and force actually refer to.

themes.name: Living on Your Own Terms
themes.tagline: One woman's quiet rebellion against the timeline everyone assumed you were following.

items.title: thoughts on not being in a relationship until the ripe age of 30
items.description: shop our HOWL-O-WEEN collection here: https://www.etsy.com/shop/Luxulite
items.why_watch: Karolina Żebrowska, known for her sharp cultural commentary, reflects on reaching her 30s without having been in a relationship — not as a confession, but as a considered perspective on what that experience actually taught her. Her videos consistently resist the expected narrative arc, and this one is likely no different. Worth it if you appreciate introspection delivered with dry wit rather than self-help framing.

morning_soundtrack.title: Alex Ferreira: Tiny Desk Concert
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The Dominican singer raises the everyday to a level of artistic beauty, yet manages to make life feel breathable. Silvana Estrada guests in this stripped down set.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like catching sunlight through a kitchen window while someone you love hums in the next room.

morning_soundtrack.title: Bonniesongs – “Scream”
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Bonniesongs is the musical moniker of Irish-born, Australian-based multi-instrumentalist Bonnie Stewart, who has classified her off-kilter songwriting as "ethereal grunge." Today, she returned with a peculiar banger called "Scream."
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The sound of a music box that learned to scream — delicate, deranged, and oddly compelling.

morning_soundtrack.title: Julia Jacklin On Chaos, Control, And The Gem
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Julia Jacklin is changing her mind. There’s power in that. When I spoke with the Melbourne-based musician about her last album Pre Pleasure , in 2022, she imagined that her future self might approach music with more calculation.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The artistic equivalent of rearranging the furniture at 2am and realizing it finally feels right.

morning_soundtrack.title: Strand Of Oaks’ Timothy Showalter Cast In Prison Break Spinoff Following Sons Of Anarchy Spinoff
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Timothy Showalter makes soulfully scraggly indie rock as Strand Of Oaks, and he seems to have a nice little side hustle adding his own soulfully scraggly presence to various television spinoffs. Back in 2022, Showalter was cast in a recurring role as a character named Hoosier on the Sons Of Anarchy spinoff Mayans M.C. (Showalter really is from Indiana, so the name fit.) Showalter was on 10 episodes of that show. I didn't watch that show, but I was not surprised to learn, looking it up just now, that his character got murdered.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The rare energy of a man equally at home writing heartland rock ballads and getting dramatically murdered on cable TV.

morning_soundtrack.title: THE READING ROOM: John Krajicek’s ‘Patience for the Ride: The Art and Life of Will Johnson’
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Linda Ronstadt once told me that when she records a song, she keeps an art book open on the music stand in front of her. The pages of paintings inspired her in their breadth, illustrating the multi-faceted artistic response to, and interpretation of, the world around us. Those visual
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The feeling of thumbing through a worn paperback in a used record store while something quietly brilliant plays overhead.

morning_soundtrack.title: ALBUM REVIEW: Leon Bridges Delivers an Ode to Joy on 'Happiness Anytime'
morning_soundtrack.snippet: With his exuberant soul stylings, his upbeat dance rhythms, and his velvety vocals, Leon Bridges dispenses a heart-nourishing dose of joyous soul on his appropriately titled new album Happiness Anytime . Produced by Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto of Jungle, Bridges’ 12-song collection — much of
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like a second line parade spilling out of a church and straight into your bloodstream on a hot afternoon.

morning_soundtrack.title: Michael Kiwanuka Serves Up New Album Fudge
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The self-produced LP was written “almost concurrently” with 2024’s Small Changes
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The sonic texture of a velvet couch in a dimly lit room where something quietly revelatory is always about to happen.

morning_soundtrack.title: Sebadoh Reissuing Harmacy for 30th Anniversary
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Listen to one of five previously unreleased additions, an alternate version of “Beauty of the Ride”
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Basement-tape nostalgia with the particular ache of rediscovering a mixtape from a version of yourself you'd almost forgotten.

morning_soundtrack.title: Dungen :: Vidrig Vår
morning_soundtrack.snippet: On the veteran Swedish outfit's most pared down and elegant affair, Vidrig Vår showcases Dungen still operating on a psychedelic wavelength not found elsewhere. Built around bandleader Gustav Ejste's panoramic piano progressions, the ballad-centric record flows with the weightless springtime atmosphere of the band's organically cinematic orbit. The post Dungen :: Vidrig Vår first appeared on Aquarium Drunkard .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like watching frost melt off a window pane in slow motion while a Mellotron plays somewhere just out of sight.

morning_soundtrack.title: Asher White :: Love Aggregates
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Asher White goes maximalist on Love Aggregates , building heavy doses of orchestral power pop from her bedroom. A fragmentary heartbreak album touching on dysphoria, precarious labor, Jerry Garcia, Citi Bikes, and Flatbush in the snow, it transforms intimate falsettos, arpeggiating guitars, and toy piano melodies into a luminous, redemptive vision of love. The post Asher White :: Love Aggregates first appeared on Aquarium Drunkard .
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Heartbreak reconstructed from spare parts — toy pianos, city slush, and a stubborn, luminous hope.

morning_soundtrack.title: Those Were the Days of Miracle and Wonder :: Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Paul Simon’s 1986 album Graceland exists in this weird state, an album that eternally evokes 1986, but always sounds so different from other albums of its era. It’s an collection that’s self absorbed, but also so relatable when the listener finds themselves hitting middle age. It brought world music to the forefront, but also presented a misleading picture.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The bittersweet vertigo of an album that makes middle age feel like both a wound and a miracle.

morning_soundtrack.title: Bruce Springsteen’s Rejected “Dancing in the Dark” Music Video Heads to Auction
morning_soundtrack.snippet: The original master sat in former Columbia Records president Al Teller's file cabinet for more than four decades. Bruce Springsteen’s Rejected “Dancing in the Dark” Music Video Heads to Auction Karan Singh
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The ghost of a neon-lit 1984 that almost was, rattling around in a filing cabinet for forty years.

global_silver_linings.title: Teens Set World Record for Most Sports Balls Recycled in One Day, Diverting 2,675 Pounds from Landfills
global_silver_linings.snippet: In March, GNN reported on the attempt by teens to set a Guinness World Record for the most racquet sport balls recycled in a single day, and we’re happy to tell you: they pulled it off. It took awhile, but last weekend a group of teen environmentalists from California collected about 22,000 mostly pickle and […]
global_silver_linings.reason: A group of teenagers proved that young people can turn a simple idea into real environmental impact, keeping over a ton of worn-out sports equipment out of landfills in a single day. It's a reminder that meaningful action doesn't require waiting for someone older or more powerful to lead the way.

global_silver_linings.title: California man’s parents died in 2020 and 2022. He just received a postcard in the mail from them.
global_silver_linings.reason: A postcard sent with love found its way home years later, offering an unexpected moment of connection across grief and time. It's a quiet, tender reminder that the bonds we share with the people we love have a way of reaching us when we need them most.

global_silver_linings.title: The tilcayo: new wildcat species discovered in Bolivia’s cloud forest
global_silver_linings.snippet: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For years, biologists cataloguing Bolivia’s Yungas cloud forest would note a small spotted cat and move on. Tiger cat, broadly speaking. The general profile fit and there was no obvious reason to dig further.
global_silver_linings.reason: The discovery of a previously unknown wildcat species in Bolivia's cloud forest is a heartening sign that Earth still holds secrets worth protecting — and that dedicated researchers are out there finding them. Every new species uncovered strengthens the case for preserving the wild places that shelter life we haven't even met yet.

discovery_articles.title: The Press Mosaic in Baku, Azerbaijan
discovery_articles.snippet: The building that printed Soviet Azerbaijan's newspapers and books is shaped like an open book. It takes a moment to register from the pavement, and then it becomes difficult to see anything else: two great pages picked out in cut stone, spread wide across the front of the printing house. Worked into them is a history of writing.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Someone decided that a building devoted to the printed word should itself become a book — and then carved the entire history of writing into its stone pages. It's the kind of architectural joke that takes a century to land properly.

discovery_articles.title: Replica of the Portal of the Casa de la Cadena in Navalcarnero, Spain
discovery_articles.snippet: Navalcarnero may be a small town southwest of Madrid, but its streets are steeped in history. Founded in the 15th century, it became an important stop between Madrid and Toledo and is now particularly celebrated for its wine production. The town's vineyards form part of the Denomination of Origin Vinos de Madrid, and its winemaking tradition has long been one of Navalcarnero's defining features.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The replica portal is almost a footnote here, overshadowed by the quiet fact that this small town once held the thread between two of Spain's greatest cities — and chose to remember itself through wine instead. Some towns know exactly who they are.

discovery_articles.title: House of the Gladiators in Episkopi, Cyprus
discovery_articles.snippet: Kourion's ruins are full of mosaics: mythological scenes, geometric patterns, hunting parties. But tucked near the main courtyard of one villa is something the rest of the island almost never shows: gladiators, fighting, identified by name. According to Cyprus's own Department of Antiquities, gladiatorial combat is a rare subject for mosaic art anywhere on the island, which is what gives this otherwise modest 3rd-century house its name.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: In a place blanketed with mythological mosaics, someone in 3rd-century Cyprus commissioned a floor featuring named gladiators mid-fight — specific, violent, and almost nowhere else on the island. The names are what haunt: these weren't symbols, they were people someone thought worth remembering.

discovery_articles.title: Why Did Claude Monet Paint the Same Scenes Over and Over Again? The Impressionist Artist Was Obsessed With Capturing the Fleeting Nature of Time
discovery_articles.snippet: An upcoming exhibition at Tate Modern will feature more than 60 artworks created by Monet between the 1870s and 1920s. These pieces reveal how he documented changing light and weather conditions
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Monet wasn't painting haystacks — he was painting time itself dissolving, returning to the same subject dozens of times because the light never repeated and he knew it. What looks like an obsession was really a very quiet argument with impermanence.

discovery_articles.title: Scientists Say Scorching Temperatures Brought on by the 'Super' El Niño Could Kill Nearly Half a Million People by February
discovery_articles.snippet: The predicted number, which includes deaths since June, likely represents an underestimate of total deaths. The heat could linger beyond February, and the climate swing could bring about other life-threatening conditions, including flooding, wildfire and infectious diseases
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The number half a million is staggering enough, but the quieter horror is the parenthetical: this likely undercounts, because the heat may simply keep going. We are, it turns out, quite bad at imagining the end of a thing that hasn't ended yet.

discovery_articles.title: A Metal Detectorist Exploring a Field in Germany Was Stunned to Discover a Massive Hoard of Roman Coins
discovery_articles.snippet: Together, the 943 silver denarii span nearly 300 years of Roman history, from 148 B.C.E. to 124 or 125 C.E.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Nine hundred and forty-three silver coins spanning nearly three centuries of Roman history, buried in a German field and found by someone with a metal detector on an ordinary afternoon. The Romans who hid them never came back, and for almost two thousand years neither did anyone else.

discovery_articles.title: During the American Revolution, the City of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, Served as the United States' Capital for Just One Day
discovery_articles.snippet: The nascent nation's leaders fled to the inland city as the British advanced on Philadelphia in September 1777. They held one meeting at the local courthouse before moving on to York
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The United States once had a capital for exactly one day — a single courthouse meeting in Lancaster before everyone moved on, as if the nation itself was still deciding whether to exist. It's the most provisional founding you've never been taught.

discovery_articles.title: Meet the newest living cat species, the first described in 100 years
discovery_articles.snippet: Genetic testing of two tiny tiger cats from Bolivia revealed a new species, adding a new branch to the feline family tree.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: A new cat species — the first described in a century — was hiding in Bolivia in plain sight, waiting for a DNA test to tell us it wasn't what we thought it was. The feline family tree quietly grew a branch, and the cats, presumably, are unbothered.

discovery_articles.title: This year’s El Niño just broke a record months before it’s expected to peak
discovery_articles.snippet: Daily sea surface temperatures in the region where El Niño develops are more extreme than at any point in recorded history.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Sea surface temperatures are now more extreme than at any recorded point in history, and El Niño hasn't even peaked yet — which means we're measuring a record that is still being broken while we write about it. The thermometer, it turns out, has no ceiling we've found.

discovery_articles.title: Teaching Students to Follow an Idea
discovery_articles.snippet: A five-step classroom exercise reframes research as an evolving scholarly conversation rather than a search for sources.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: The most radical thing this classroom exercise does is reframe research not as finding answers but as entering a conversation already in progress — which is, quietly, how all real thinking actually works. Students who learn this early are quietly handed a key most people never find.

discovery_articles.title: Red Moons and Lightning Illuminate Sarah Lee’s Uncanny Landscapes
discovery_articles.snippet: Supple mountains cradled by lakes and forests are tinged with magical realism.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Sarah Lee's landscapes feel like places that exist just past the edge of memory — mountains you almost recognize, skies lit by something not quite lightning. They're the visual equivalent of a word on the tip of your tongue.

featured_read.title: How Social Learning Keeps Orangutans Fed
featured_read.snippet: Orangutans learn by watching, then trying
featured_read.blurb: This piece follows orangutans through the quiet, patient act of watching one another — and asks what it really means to learn something worth knowing. It turns out culture isn't uniquely human; it's also a matter of who you sit next to at lunch.

reading_room.title: The evil eye is irrational. Abandon it at your peril
reading_room.snippet: So many of the world’s superstitions have been supplanted by rational thinking. Why does one of the oldest beliefs persist? - by Timna Abramov Read on Psyche
reading_room.blurb: Timna Abramov takes one of humanity's oldest anxieties — the fear that someone's envy can genuinely harm you — and asks why no amount of modernity has managed to kill it off. The answer says something uncomfortably true about the limits of reason.

reading_room.title: John Berger, Death’s Secretary: A Conversation with Tom Overton
reading_room.snippet: “The first letter I sent to him was about a print that he’d made, which was in the archive—a Chagall-inspired Virgin Mary standing on a donkey.”
reading_room.blurb: Tom Overton spent years inside John Berger's archive and correspondence, and this conversation circles a tender, strange question: what does it mean to be the keeper of a great thinker's unfinished thoughts? A portrait of literary friendship built letter by careful letter.

reading_room.title: Heaven’s Melodic Strains
reading_room.snippet: "From a certain height, the problem becomes one of knowledge itself: Do you believe what you hear, or do you hear what you believe?"
reading_room.blurb: This essay wraps itself around the unsettling idea that listening is never quite neutral — that what we hear is already shaped by what we've decided to believe. Set aside the half-hour; it rewards a slow, quiet read.

reading_room.title: I’m Having a Hard Time Saying No: How Can I Be More of a Literary Asshole?
reading_room.snippet: Well, hello there! Welcome back, friends. You’ve arrived at the very best destination in town.
reading_room.blurb: A candid, funny reckoning with the writer's chronic inability to say no — and the surprising cost of being too agreeable in a literary world that mistakes niceness for weakness. Consider it permission to disappoint someone this week.

reading_room.title: Now Entering: The Era Of Bleh
reading_room.blurb: Neither burnout nor depression nor dread — just a pervasive, low-grade flatness that seems to be the defining mood of right now. This piece tries to name the feeling precisely, which is itself a small relief.

garden_note.note: Zürich's evenings are taking on that particular amber quality now — the light thickening like honey before the sun slips away at 19:21, and the linden trees beginning their slow bronze turn along the Limmat. This is the quiet fulcrum of early autumn: the kitchen garden still generous, the air already carrying that faint mineral coolness that reminds you winter is merely resting.
